title: Stage 9, Lesson 6: Life insurance - term or whole life?
subtitle: Two very different philosophies, not one product under two names
openingQuestion: What is the core difference between term life insurance and whole life insurance?
openingOptions: Term covers a fixed period at a low premium; whole life covers you for life
The two are identical and differ only in the marketing name
Whole life is always cheaper than term because it covers longer
Term is only for older people, while whole life is only sold to younger ones
explanation: Term life is pure protection - a low premium, a payout if the insured dies within the contract term (5, 10, 20 years), and nothing accumulated if the term ends without a claim. Whole life combines lifelong protection with a savings or investment component inside the contract, which is why the premium is several times higher than term at the same level of cover.

diagram.label: Term life: low premium, fixed period, no accumulation
Whole life: high premium, lifelong cover, accumulated value

realWorldExample.company: The "buy term, invest the difference" strategy
realWorldExample.description: Many personal finance advisers recommend buying cheap term life for the cover actually needed, then investing the premium difference against whole life elsewhere - because the "accumulation" inside a whole life policy usually carries high management costs and returns that do not compete with investing directly.

quiz.question: A young family on a modest income with a large mortgage should prioritise which type of life cover?
options: An investment-linked policy, to protect and earn at the same time
Whole life, because it accumulates a surrender value for later on
Term life at a level of cover that would clear the mortgage
No cover at all yet, while the income is still modest
quiz.explanation: The stage with a large debt (a mortgage) and dependants (young children) but limited income and savings is when protection is MOST needed and the BUDGET is tightest - term life at a sufficient level of cover solves exactly that at the lowest cost.

quiz.question: Why do personal finance advisers usually rate the "accumulated value" inside a whole life policy as inefficient compared with investing separately?
options: The insurer keeps all of the investment return on that portion
The accumulated value is taxed at a very high personal rate
The accumulated value cannot be withdrawn before maturity
Management charges and embedded insurance costs erode it
quiz.explanation: A whole life contract bundles the cost of insurance, the management charges and the accumulation into a single product - a fee structure that is usually less transparent and more expensive than separating them: cheap term life for protection, and the surplus invested where the costs are visible.

quiz.question: When is someone's need for life cover usually at its highest?
options: While the mortgage is large and the children are young
On first starting work, with nobody yet depending on your income
Once accumulated wealth reaches its lifetime peak
Just after retiring, with no salary coming in
quiz.explanation: Life insurance protects the people who depend on your income. The need peaks exactly when the financial obligations are largest and the accumulated assets smallest, then falls away over time.

quiz.question: What is the core idea behind "buy pure protection and invest the difference"?
options: Buy term, then use the surplus to prepay the mortgage
Separate protection from investing so each can be optimised
Only buy cover once the investments have run long enough to profit
Bundle protection and investing into one contract for simplicity
quiz.explanation: When two purposes are bundled into one product, it is very hard to see how much you are paying for protection and how much for investing. Separating them makes costs comparable - but it demands the discipline to actually invest the difference rather than spend it.

quiz.question: How do you roughly estimate how much life cover to buy?
options: By the total premiums you expect to pay across the whole contract term
By about ten times annual income, applied uniformly to every single family situation
Enough to clear the debts and support dependants until they can support themselves
By the value of your current assets, so heirs keep that block of wealth intact
quiz.explanation: Life cover replaces the income dependants lose, so the amount tracks the specific obligations: the mortgage balance, the cost of raising children to adulthood. One consequence people miss: that need falls as the debt shrinks and the children grow.

keyTakeaways: Term life: low premium, fixed period, pure protection - suited to the stage where protection needs are high and the budget is limited
Whole life: a far higher premium, lifelong cover, with accumulated value that hidden costs usually make inefficient as an investment
The common strategy: buy enough term for the need, and invest the premium difference yourself

practicePrompt.question: You compare two life policies with the same 2 billion of cover: term life at 3 million a year, whole life at 25 million a year. Why is the gap so wide when the cover is identical?
options: Term is cheaper because it is pure protection; whole life also builds a cash value
This is a pricing error at the insurer; two policies with the same cover should carry the same premium
Whole life is dearer only because the contract term is longer, with nothing to do with the product structure
Term is cheaper because its real cover is far below the 2 billion figure that is advertised
practicePrompt.explanation: Term life costs far less than whole life at the same level of cover because there is no accumulation inside it. The common strategy: buy enough term for the need, and invest the premium difference yourself.

application.title: Work out the cover you need, then pick the type
application.message: Add the outstanding debt, the household's living costs multiplied by the years your children remain dependent, and the expected school fees; subtract the liquid assets you hold. That figure is the cover you need. Choose the product afterwards, rather than choosing first and then asking how much it covers.
application.secondary: If an adviser only asks how much you can pay a year and never asks how much your family would need, the conversation is running backwards.

sections.text: Term life and whole life are not two versions of one product - they serve two entirely different philosophies.
Term life: pure protection at a low premium

Term life covers a defined period at a low premium, with no accumulated value if the term ends without a claim. Whole life combines lifelong cover with an accumulation component, but the premium is several times higher and the embedded management costs usually make it less efficient than investing the premium difference separately. For a young family with a large mortgage and modest income, term life at a sufficient level of cover is usually the more sensible choice.

items: Term life: low premium, fixed period, no accumulation - suited to a stage with high protection needs and a limited budget
Whole life: a far higher premium, with accumulation that hidden costs usually make inefficient as an investment
The common strategy: buy enough term for the need, and invest the premium difference yourself

sections.text: The first question is not which product but how much. A simple estimate: add up the financial obligations that would not disappear if you did - the mortgage balance, the living costs of your dependants across the years they still need support, the school fees you expect - then subtract the liquid assets you already hold. The difference is the cover you need. That number moves over time: it peaks while the mortgage is large and the children are small, then falls as the debt clears and they become independent.

sections.title: Estimating the cover needed
sections.equation: Cover needed = Outstanding debt + Dependants' living costs × Years + Expected school fees − Liquid assets

example.title: A young family
example.calculation: 1.5 billion of mortgage + (15 million a month × 12 × 10 years = 1.8 billion) + 500 million of fees − 300 million of savings
example.explanation: This is the level of cover that keeps the family from having to sell the home and lets them maintain their life for roughly ten years. The figure falls year by year as the mortgage shrinks and the savings grow.

left.label: Term life
left.text: The low premium means the same budget buys several times more cover. Nothing comes back at the end of the term - exactly what pure protection is, like car insurance or fire cover.

right.label: Whole life
right.text: Lifelong cover with an accumulation component, but several times the premium for the same cover. The accumulation bears management charges and usually takes years before the surrender value amounts to much.

items: For the same annual premium, how many times apart are the payouts of the two product types?
On a policy with accumulation: what is the surrender value after 5 and 10 years, and how many years before it equals the premiums paid in?
Which circumstances are excluded from payout, and what are the conditions on declaring your health?
If you cannot keep paying the premium after a few years, what happens - does the policy lapse, or convert into something else?

sections.label: One direct way to ask
sections.text: Ask the adviser to produce an illustration of two options at the same annual premium: one pure protection contract and one with accumulation. Side by side, the difference in payout and in money returned becomes very clear, and you can decide for yourself which matters more in your circumstances.

lines: Life insurance should answer "who would be financially affected if I died", not "which product sounds most attractive".
For most young families, plain term life is still the most effective choice.

summary.keyIdea: Term life: low premium, fixed period, pure protection - suited to the stage where protection needs are high and the budget is limited
summary.commonMistake: Easy to skip: whole life carries a far higher premium and lifelong cover with accumulated value, but hidden costs usually make that accumulation inefficient
summary.action: The common strategy: buy enough term for the need, and invest the premium difference yourself
